name: Ink in Water
note: Cites suminagashi but does not model lifting the pattern onto paper.

lumenary.blurb: Drops of ink released into still water curl and bloom along slow currents. Each wisp carries the colour of the picture where it was released. Drag across the water to add ink.

facts.bestOn: Colourful pictures, where the ink takes colour

why: Ink in still water does two things at once. Slow currents carry it along, and diffusion spreads it out. Real water moves without bunching up or leaving gaps, so the ink curls and blooms in long wisps. The program uses a flow with that same property, and each wisp carries the colour of the picture where it was released.
how: Release a drop as a burst of about 380 particles (times the ink slider) in a disc 9 px across, each with a small outward push.
Carry every particle with a flow from curl noise: if ψ is smooth noise, the velocity v = (∂ψ/∂y, −∂ψ/∂x) has zero divergence, so the flow is incompressible.
Measure the gradient by central differences over 6 px and damp the velocity by 0.9 per step so particles follow the current.
Give each particle the colour of the picture where it was released and draw up to 6,500 of them as translucent, soft sprites.
Fade the ink slowly, by the linger value, so old wisps thin out.
history: Suminagashi, the Japanese art of floating ink on water and lifting the pattern onto paper, dates to the twelfth century. In 1883 Osborne Reynolds released a thread of dye in a glass pipe to show how smooth flow turns into turbulence. Robert Bridson, Jim Hourihan and Marcus Nordenstam introduced curl noise to computer graphics in 2007 as a cheap way to make convincing fluid motion.
uses: Smoke, fluid and magic effects in film and games
terms: Being carried along by a flow.
Spreading out from a crowded place to an emptier one.
Noise turned into a flow that never bunches up.
paragraphs: Ink in still water spreads by two means: it is carried along by slow currents (advection) and it diffuses. The program uses up to 6,500 ink particles. A drop is a burst of about 380 particles (times the ink-in-each-drop slider) in a small disc 9 px across, each given a small outward push. Every particle is carried by a flow made from curl noise. If ψ(x, y, t) is a smooth scalar noise, the velocity v = (∂ψ/∂y, −∂ψ/∂x) has zero divergence, which means the flow is incompressible. The ink therefore swirls and curls without bunching up or leaving gaps, as real ink in water does. The gradient is measured by central differences over 6 px, the velocity is damped by 0.9 per step so it follows the currents with some inertia, and a little random jitter and a gentle sinking are added.

Each particle draws a translucent disc on a persistent canvas whose radius grows as 1 + 0.45 × its age, with an opacity of 0.07 (1 − age/life)^0.6, so the layers add up as 1 − Π(1 − a) and darken where the ink is thick. The ink’s colour is that of the picture where the drop was released, made 1.5 times as saturated and set to 0.82 of its brightness on light water or 1.25 of it on dark water, so each drop is a distinct hue. The release spot is chosen from six random candidates as the one with the most colour (largest difference between its strongest and weakest channel). The canvas is pulled back toward the water colour at every frame, by 7% down to 0.3% per frame at 30 per second according to how long the ink lingers. Moving the pointer across the water releases small drops.

equations.note: Curl noise: ψ is smooth noise that also drifts with time, F the strength of the currents.
Layered translucent discs; q is the ink-per-drop slider.
The ink thins out: ℓ is the linger slider.

presets.text: Strong currents and long lingering ink make dramatic ribbons.
Ink on a dark pool glows.
